title: Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP)
body:
Terminology and evidence frame. HIV is the virus (human immunodeficiency virus); AIDS is the syndrome (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) that can follow untreated HIV infection, so prevention in this database means interrupting HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the small number of stem-cell-transplant cases with sustained remission reported in the research literature are research exceptions involving high-risk procedures, not available cures. No prevention method described here is fully effective in real-world use; effectiveness figures below are conditional on adherence, correct use, and follow-up testing. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for individual advice.

Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is the use of antiretroviral agents by HIV-negative individuals to prevent acquisition. Standard oral regimens combine tenofovir disoproxil fumarate with emtricitabine (TDF/FTC), or tenofovir alafenamide with emtricitabine (TAF/FTC) for sexual exposure in specified populations. Long-acting injectable cabotegravir, administered intramuscularly every two months after initiation, is an alternative where licensed. Event-driven (2-1-1) dosing is an option for some men who have sex with men in some guidelines, but it is not recommended for all exposure types.

The mechanism is pre-loading of target tissues with antiretrovirals so that reverse transcription of incoming virus is blocked before systemic infection is established. Tenofovir diphosphate and emtricitabine triphosphate act as nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors. Because protection depends on drug concentration at the exposure site, adherence is the dominant determinant of effectiveness: rectal tissue reaches protective concentrations faster than vaginal tissue, which is why daily dosing and adherence counseling are emphasized for vaginal exposure.

In trials and open-label studies, daily oral TDF/FTC reduced sexually acquired HIV risk by roughly 99 percent among participants with drug levels consistent with daily use, while intention-to-treat estimates were lower because of missed doses. The HPTN 083 trial found injectable cabotegravir superior to daily oral TDF/FTC in the study populations, largely reflecting adherence differences. PrEP has no activity against other sexually transmitted infections, and breakthrough infections, though uncommon with good adherence, remain possible, so periodic HIV testing, kidney-function monitoring, and sexually transmitted infection screening are part of standard follow-up.

Access routes include sexual-health clinics, primary care, and telehealth programs, with generic TDF/FTC lowering cost in many settings. Baseline requirements include a negative HIV test, kidney-function assessment, hepatitis B screening, and pregnancy considerations where relevant. Limitations include adherence dependence, a tail period of declining drug levels after stopping injectable PrEP during which alternative prevention is advised, and the need for ongoing engagement with care. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for regimen selection and monitoring.

print('PrEP lowers risk greatly when taken as prescribed; it is not fully effective and does not protect against other STIs.')

title: Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP)
body:
Terminology and evidence frame. HIV is the virus (human immunodeficiency virus); AIDS is the syndrome (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) that can follow untreated HIV infection, so prevention in this database means interrupting HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the small number of stem-cell-transplant cases with sustained remission reported in the research literature are research exceptions involving high-risk procedures, not available cures. No prevention method described here is fully effective in real-world use; effectiveness figures below are conditional on adherence, correct use, and follow-up testing. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for individual advice.

Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is a 28-day course of combination antiretroviral therapy initiated after a potential HIV exposure to prevent establishment of infection. Indications include condomless sex with a partner of unknown or positive status, condom failure, sexual assault, and occupational or non-occupational percutaneous or mucosal exposures. Standard regimens combine an integrase inhibitor with two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, selected according to local guidelines, resistance considerations, and the exposed person's other conditions.

The biological rationale is time-critical: antiretrovirals must reach target cells and block reverse transcription before viral dissemination and reservoir seeding. Animal and observational human data support a steep decline in benefit with delay, and no benefit is expected beyond 72 hours, which is the accepted outer limit for initiation. Baseline HIV testing is required so that PEP is not mistaken for treatment of established infection, and testing for hepatitis B and C, other sexually transmitted infections, and pregnancy is included where relevant.

Effectiveness cannot be quantified by a randomized trial in humans for ethical reasons; observational data, including a classic case-control study of health-care workers, suggest substantial risk reduction when started promptly and completed. Adherence across 28 days is the main modifiable factor, and gastrointestinal side effects are the commonest reason for discontinuation. PEP is not a substitute for PrEP in people with ongoing risk: after PEP, clinicians assess whether PrEP is appropriate.

Access is through emergency departments, urgent-care and sexual-health services, and occupational-health programs, with 24-hour availability in many systems. Limitations include the narrow time window, side-effect burden, drug-interaction checks, and the need for follow-up testing at intervals set by the treating service, typically including a test after the course and again later to cover the window period. Anyone with a possible exposure should seek emergency care immediately and see a clinician or an HIV testing service for follow-up.

title: Condoms
body:
Terminology and evidence frame. HIV is the virus (human immunodeficiency virus); AIDS is the syndrome (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) that can follow untreated HIV infection, so prevention in this database means interrupting HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the small number of stem-cell-transplant cases with sustained remission reported in the research literature are research exceptions involving high-risk procedures, not available cures. No prevention method described here is fully effective in real-world use; effectiveness figures below are conditional on adherence, correct use, and follow-up testing. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for individual advice.

Condoms, external (male) and internal (female), are barrier devices that prevent mucosal contact with infectious fluids during sex. Latex, polyurethane, and polyisoprene are the usual materials; natural-membrane condoms are not recommended for infection prevention because of porosity. Correct use requires application before genital contact, adequate lubrication, withdrawal while holding the base, and single use with disposal after each act.

The mechanism is straightforward physical exclusion: an intact condom prevents semen, cervicovaginal secretions, and blood from reaching susceptible mucosal surfaces and micro-abrasions. Laboratory testing shows latex and synthetic condoms are impermeable to HIV-sized particles when intact. Failure modes are breakage, slippage, and user error, including late application, reuse, and use of oil-based lubricants with latex.

Perfect-use studies estimate very high protection against HIV transmission, while typical-use effectiveness is lower because of inconsistent or incorrect use. Population-level estimates therefore depend on the proportion of acts protected and on correct use. Condoms additionally reduce transmission of other sexually transmitted infections to varying degrees depending on whether the infection site is covered, and they provide contraception for vaginal sex. They do not protect skin areas outside the barrier.

Access is over the counter and through free-distribution programs, with no prescription required in most settings. Limitations include user dependence, reduced acceptability for some people, latex allergy (addressed by synthetic alternatives), and the need for negotiation between partners. Condom promotion is commonly combined with testing, PrEP, and treatment programs. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for demonstrations and for advice on combining methods.

title: Regular HIV Testing
body:
Terminology and evidence frame. HIV is the virus (human immunodeficiency virus); AIDS is the syndrome (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) that can follow untreated HIV infection, so prevention in this database means interrupting HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the small number of stem-cell-transplant cases with sustained remission reported in the research literature are research exceptions involving high-risk procedures, not available cures. No prevention method described here is fully effective in real-world use; effectiveness figures below are conditional on adherence, correct use, and follow-up testing. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for individual advice.

Regular HIV testing is the scheduled, repeated use of HIV assays in people at risk, independent of symptoms. Because acute and early HIV infection is frequently asymptomatic, routine testing is the mechanism by which infections are detected early enough for treatment initiation and transmission prevention. Testing programs use laboratory-based antigen/antibody immunoassays, differentiation assays, and nucleic acid tests (NAT), alongside point-of-care rapid antibody and antigen/antibody tests.

Terminology matters here and throughout this database: HIV is the virus, AIDS is the syndrome that can follow untreated HIV infection, and prevention means stopping HIV transmission. Assay performance is defined by the window period: NAT detects HIV RNA roughly 10 to 33 days after infection, laboratory antigen/antibody tests roughly 18 to 45 days, and antibody-only tests roughly 23 to 90 days, with individual variation. A reactive screening result requires confirmatory testing under the laboratory algorithm before a diagnosis is made; a single rapid result is never treated as final on its own.

Testing effectiveness as a prevention tool is indirect but well supported: diagnosis enables antiretroviral therapy, which suppresses viral load and prevents onward sexual transmission, and it triggers partner services and prevention counseling. The limits are the window period, the need for retesting after recent exposure, and linkage failures when a positive result does not lead promptly to care. Self-testing extends reach but requires a clear route to confirmatory laboratory testing and linkage.

Access includes clinical services, community-based testing, and self-test distribution programs, with opt-out testing recommended for everyone aged 13 to 64 at least once in many national guidelines. Confidentiality protections and, in some services, anonymous testing reduce barriers. Anyone with a recent possible exposure should see a clinician or an HIV testing service promptly, since PEP decisions depend on timing and cannot wait for a routine test date.

title: Treatment as Prevention and U=U
body:
Terminology and evidence frame. HIV is the virus (human immunodeficiency virus); AIDS is the syndrome (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) that can follow untreated HIV infection, so prevention in this database means interrupting HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the small number of stem-cell-transplant cases with sustained remission reported in the research literature are research exceptions involving high-risk procedures, not available cures. No prevention method described here is fully effective in real-world use; effectiveness figures below are conditional on adherence, correct use, and follow-up testing. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for individual advice.

Treatment as prevention (TasP) is the use of antiretroviral therapy (ART) in people with HIV to suppress plasma HIV RNA and thereby prevent onward transmission. U=U, undetectable equals untransmittable, expresses the finding that a person with a sustained undetectable viral load, conventionally below 200 copies per milliliter, does not transmit HIV sexually. ART regimens typically combine an integrase inhibitor with two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors and block viral replication at several steps.

The mechanism is suppression of viral replication in blood and genital compartments below the threshold required for transmission. HPTN 052, a randomized trial in serodiscordant couples, showed early ART reduced linked transmissions by about 96 percent, and the observational PARTNER and PARTNER2 studies recorded no linked sexual transmissions across tens of thousands of condomless sex acts when the partner with HIV was virally suppressed. The evidence base is therefore strongest for sexual transmission under durable suppression with regular viral-load monitoring.

Effectiveness is conditional, not absolute: it requires adherence, durable suppression for at least six months by most definitions, and continued monitoring, since treatment interruptions, drug resistance, or intercurrent illness can allow viral rebound. U=U does not apply to transmission through shared injection equipment, where blood exposure differs, nor does it remove the need for antenatal and perinatal measures in pregnancy. It also does not protect against other sexually transmitted infections.

Access depends on diagnosis, linkage to HIV care, and sustained medicine supply, all of which remain uneven globally. Limitations include adherence burden, side effects, drug interactions, stigma, and health-system gaps that interrupt supply. TasP is a population-level prevention strategy only insofar as testing, linkage, and retention in care succeed. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for testing, treatment initiation, and viral-load monitoring.

title: Needle and Syringe Safety and Harm-Reduction Services
body:
Terminology and evidence frame. HIV is the virus (human immunodeficiency virus); AIDS is the syndrome (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) that can follow untreated HIV infection, so prevention in this database means interrupting HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the small number of stem-cell-transplant cases with sustained remission reported in the research literature are research exceptions involving high-risk procedures, not available cures. No prevention method described here is fully effective in real-world use; effectiveness figures below are conditional on adherence, correct use, and follow-up testing. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for individual advice.

Parenteral HIV transmission occurs when blood containing HIV is introduced through shared injection equipment. Effective prevention therefore requires sterile needles and syringes for every injection, sterile ancillary equipment (cookers, filters, water), and safe disposal through sharps containers. Syringe services programs (SSPs) operationalize this by distributing sterile equipment, collecting used sharps, and bundling testing for HIV, hepatitis B and C, vaccination, wound care, and referral to medication for opioid use disorder and to HIV care.

The mechanism is interruption of blood-borne exposure: a sterile needle and syringe contain no residual blood, so the transmission route is closed for that injection. SSPs add a second mechanism, engagement: regular, non-judgmental contact brings people who inject drugs into testing and treatment systems they might otherwise avoid. Modeling and observational studies consistently associate SSP access with lower HIV incidence among people who inject drugs and with higher rates of HIV testing, hepatitis C treatment referral, and entry to drug treatment.

Effectiveness is partial and context-dependent: it depends on coverage (enough sterile equipment for every injection), on consistent use, and on the legal environment, since restrictive laws reduce access. SSPs do not address sexual transmission, so condoms, PrEP, and treatment as prevention remain relevant for the same population. Ancillary sharing and injection-network effects mean that individual-level sterile equipment must be paired with network-level coverage to shift incidence.

Access varies sharply by jurisdiction: some areas fund comprehensive SSPs, others restrict them or prohibit them. Where available, services are typically confidential and low-threshold. Limitations include funding instability, geographic gaps, stigma, and the need for linkage to HIV treatment and to medication for opioid use disorder. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for testing and for referral to local harm-reduction services.

title: Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission
body:
Terminology and evidence frame. HIV is the virus (human immunodeficiency virus); AIDS is the syndrome (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) that can follow untreated HIV infection, so prevention in this database means interrupting HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the small number of stem-cell-transplant cases with sustained remission reported in the research literature are research exceptions involving high-risk procedures, not available cures. No prevention method described here is fully effective in real-world use; effectiveness figures below are conditional on adherence, correct use, and follow-up testing. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for individual advice.

Mother-to-child transmission (MTCT), also called vertical transmission, occurs during pregnancy, delivery, or breastfeeding. Prevention combines routine antenatal HIV testing, antiretroviral therapy (ART) for the pregnant person with the goal of viral suppression before delivery, intrapartum measures, infant post-exposure prophylaxis, and infant-feeding guidance. Where viral suppression is achieved and sustained, transmission risk is very low; where diagnosis is late or treatment interrupted, risk rises sharply.

The mechanism is viral-load dependent: transplacental transfer, exposure to maternal blood and secretions during delivery, and ingestion of virus in breast milk are all reduced when maternal plasma and genital viral loads are suppressed. Infant prophylaxis, typically nevirapine and/or zidovudine-based regimens dosed by risk stratum, provides additional cover during the highest-risk window. Mode of delivery is individualized: with full viral suppression, vaginal delivery is generally advised, while elective caesarean section is considered at higher viral loads under some guidelines.

Without intervention, transmission risk is approximately 15 to 45 percent depending on breastfeeding duration. With comprehensive intervention, including maternal ART and infant prophylaxis, risk falls below 2 percent in non-breastfeeding settings and below 5 percent in breastfeeding populations under WHO guidance. Effectiveness is conditional on early antenatal testing, adherence, retention in care, and infant follow-up testing at recommended ages, including virological testing in infancy.

Access is through antenatal care with opt-out HIV testing, integrated prevention programs, and infant follow-up clinics. Limitations include late presentation to antenatal care, stigma, medicine stock-outs, and loss to follow-up after delivery. Infant feeding recommendations differ by setting and must follow local guidance balancing HIV risk against malnutrition and diarrhoeal risk. See a clinician or an HIV testing service early in pregnancy for testing and treatment planning.

title: Partner Services and Notification
body:
Terminology and evidence frame. HIV is the virus (human immunodeficiency virus); AIDS is the syndrome (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) that can follow untreated HIV infection, so prevention in this database means interrupting HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the small number of stem-cell-transplant cases with sustained remission reported in the research literature are research exceptions involving high-risk procedures, not available cures. No prevention method described here is fully effective in real-world use; effectiveness figures below are conditional on adherence, correct use, and follow-up testing. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for individual advice.

Partner services comprise a package of interventions offered to people diagnosed with HIV: elicitation of sexual and needle-sharing partners, notification of those partners of possible exposure, and linkage of partners to testing, treatment, or prevention. Models include patient referral (the index patient notifies), provider referral (a trained worker notifies without disclosing the source), and dual referral (both together). Contract referral sets a deadline after which the provider follows up.

The mechanism is network interruption: undiagnosed infections in a transmission network are found earlier than they would be through routine testing alone, and partners with recent exposure can be assessed for PEP within its time window or offered PrEP. Randomized and observational studies, including WHO-supported trials of assisted partner notification, found higher testing uptake and more new diagnoses with assisted approaches than with passive referral alone, with high acceptability where confidentiality was protected.

Effectiveness is conditional on confidentiality, on the index patient's willingness and safety, and on the availability of same-visit testing and linkage. Limitations include partners who cannot be located, partners who decline services, incomplete elicitation, and safety risks in the context of intimate-partner violence, for which screening and safety planning are required before notification. Partner services never disclose the source patient's identity in provider referral, and participation is voluntary.

Access is through health departments and sexual-health clinics, with services typically free. Integration with HIV testing, PrEP, and treatment programs determines whether notification converts into prevention. Anyone newly diagnosed should be offered partner services as standard care. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for confidential advice about notification options and safety planning.

title: Education and Stigma Reduction
body:
Terminology and evidence frame. HIV is the virus (human immunodeficiency virus); AIDS is the syndrome (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) that can follow untreated HIV infection, so prevention in this database means interrupting HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the small number of stem-cell-transplant cases with sustained remission reported in the research literature are research exceptions involving high-risk procedures, not available cures. No prevention method described here is fully effective in real-world use; effectiveness figures below are conditional on adherence, correct use, and follow-up testing. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for individual advice.

Education and stigma reduction are structural interventions: they alter the knowledge environment and social norms that determine whether testing, treatment, and prevention services are used. HIV-related stigma operates at internalized, interpersonal, and institutional levels, and it is associated in observational research with delayed testing, poorer treatment adherence, and avoidance of services. Interventions include curriculum-based education, contact-based programs involving people living with HIV, health-worker training, and policy reform such as anti-discrimination protections.

The mechanism is twofold. Accurate knowledge corrects transmission misconceptions, which reduces irrational avoidance and increases testing intentions. Contact and institutional reform reduce enacted stigma, which increases service uptake and retention. Evidence reviews find that multi-component programs, combining education with service access and contact, shift attitudes and testing behavior more reliably than information-only campaigns, and that fear-based messaging is ineffective or counterproductive.

Effectiveness is indirect and hard to attribute: education changes behavior only when services are available and affordable, and attitude change does not automatically produce testing or adherence. Measurement relies on stigma scales, testing uptake, and retention indicators rather than on infection endpoints alone. Programs must also avoid reinforcing stigma by framing HIV as a consequence of blameworthy behavior.

Access is through schools, clinics, workplaces, media campaigns, and community organizations. Limitations include the slow pace of norm change, backlash in hostile policy environments, and the risk of generic messaging that misses the groups most affected. Education is a necessary complement to biomedical prevention, not a substitute for it. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for accurate information and supportive referrals.

title: Safer-Sex Communication
body:
Terminology and evidence frame. HIV is the virus (human immunodeficiency virus); AIDS is the syndrome (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) that can follow untreated HIV infection, so prevention in this database means interrupting HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the small number of stem-cell-transplant cases with sustained remission reported in the research literature are research exceptions involving high-risk procedures, not available cures. No prevention method described here is fully effective in real-world use; effectiveness figures below are conditional on adherence, correct use, and follow-up testing. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for individual advice.

Safer-sex communication is the dyadic negotiation of risk-reduction behaviors before and during sex, including disclosure of testing history, agreement on condom use, discussion of PrEP or ART status, and contingency plans for condom failure. It is classified as a behavioral intervention: it does not itself block transmission but determines whether biomedical and barrier methods are actually used. Communication interventions typically teach assertiveness, scripted openers, and joint decision-making.

The mechanism is behavioral mediation: negotiated agreements increase condom-use consistency, testing frequency, and adherence support within partnerships, and they surface serodiscordance so that TasP and PrEP can be discussed. Observational research links partner communication to higher condom use and to testing uptake, while intervention trials show modest but consistent improvements in negotiated safety behaviors. Communication quality is moderated by power dynamics, gender norms, substance use, and relationship type.

Effectiveness is bounded by honesty and verification limits: self-reported status or adherence may be inaccurate, and communication cannot substitute for testing or for barrier and biomedical protection. In relationships with coercion or violence, direct negotiation may be unsafe, and safety planning takes precedence over disclosure. Communication interventions are therefore paired with service access and, where needed, with counseling and violence-support services.

Access is through sexual-health counseling, couples counseling, and community programs. Limitations include cultural and language barriers, power imbalances, and the difficulty of sustaining negotiation across casual partnerships. Communication is a complement to, never a replacement for, condoms, testing, PrEP, and treatment. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for counseling and support with partner conversations.

title: Voluntary Medical Male Circumcision
body:
Terminology and evidence frame. HIV is the virus (human immunodeficiency virus); AIDS is the syndrome (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) that can follow untreated HIV infection, so prevention in this database means interrupting HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the small number of stem-cell-transplant cases with sustained remission reported in the research literature are research exceptions involving high-risk procedures, not available cures. No prevention method described here is fully effective in real-world use; effectiveness figures below are conditional on adherence, correct use, and follow-up testing. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for individual advice.

Voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) is the surgical removal of the foreskin under local anaesthesia by trained providers in clinical settings, offered as part of a comprehensive prevention package including HIV testing, counseling, condom promotion, and sexually transmitted infection management. WHO recommends VMMC as an additional prevention strategy in settings with high HIV prevalence and low circumcision prevalence, principally in eastern and southern Africa.

The mechanism is anatomical: the inner preputial mucosa is rich in Langerhans cells and CD4-positive target cells and is susceptible to micro-trauma during intercourse, providing an entry route for HIV. Removal of the foreskin reduces this susceptible surface and the moist sub-preputial environment that favors viral survival. The procedure is typically a dorsal-slit or device-based technique with a healing period of about six weeks of abstinence.

Evidence context, stated carefully: three randomized controlled trials in South Africa, Kenya, and Uganda were stopped early for efficacy, each showing approximately 60 percent reduction in female-to-male HIV acquisition. This is partial protection: it does not eliminate risk, it does not demonstrate equivalent benefit for male-to-female transmission or for receptive anal intercourse, and it does not remove the need for condoms, testing, and other prevention. Adverse events are uncommon with trained providers but include bleeding, infection, and delayed healing.

Access is through VMMC program clinics, usually free in program settings, with mandatory counseling and an HIV test offered. Limitations include the healing-period abstinence requirement, cultural acceptability, and the need for sustained program quality. VMMC is not recommended as a stand-alone strategy and never replaces condoms or treatment-based prevention. See a clinician or an HIV testing service to discuss benefits, risks, and suitability.

title: Lubricant Safety with Condoms
body:
Terminology and evidence frame. HIV is the virus (human immunodeficiency virus); AIDS is the syndrome (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) that can follow untreated HIV infection, so prevention in this database means interrupting HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the small number of stem-cell-transplant cases with sustained remission reported in the research literature are research exceptions involving high-risk procedures, not available cures. No prevention method described here is fully effective in real-world use; effectiveness figures below are conditional on adherence, correct use, and follow-up testing. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for individual advice.

Lubricant safety with condoms concerns material compatibility and friction reduction. Latex is degraded by oil-based substances: mineral oil, petroleum jelly, and plant oils disrupt the latex polymer matrix, increasing breakage risk. Water-based lubricants (glycerin- or propylene-glycol-based) and silicone-based lubricants are compatible with latex and polyurethane condoms. Polyisoprene condoms share latex's oil sensitivity. Silicone-based lubricants are incompatible with silicone devices.

The mechanism is twofold: adequate lubrication lowers the friction coefficient at the condom surface, reducing mechanical failure, particularly in anal intercourse where endogenous lubrication is absent; and compatible chemistry preserves condom tensile strength and integrity. In vitro studies show rapid latex degradation on oil exposure, and breakage surveillance links inadequate lubrication to higher failure rates. Hyperosmolar lubricants have been associated with epithelial irritation in laboratory models, which is a further reason to prefer products formulated for mucosal use.

Effectiveness is indirect: lubricant does not itself prevent HIV transmission, but it protects the effectiveness of the condom it accompanies. Limits include product availability, user preference, and the risk that numbing (anaesthetic) lubricants mask pain from condom failure or mucosal injury. Lubricant choice is therefore treated as part of condom counseling rather than as a standalone prevention method.

Access is over the counter and through condom-distribution programs. Limitations include cost, inconsistent labeling, and the need for user education about oil incompatibility. Clinicians should confirm lubricant compatibility when counseling on condom use, particularly for anal sex. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for advice on condom and lubricant combinations.

ED = 'scientific'
SAFE = {('latex', 'water-based'), ('latex', 'silicone-based'), ('polyurethane', 'water-based'), ('polyurethane', 'silicone-based'), ('polyurethane', 'oil-based')}
print('Lubricant compatibility checker — edition: ' + ED)
for condom, lube in [('latex', 'water-based'), ('latex', 'oil-based'), ('polyurethane', 'silicone-based'), ('latex', 'silicone-based')]:
    ok = (condom, lube) in SAFE
    print(condom + ' + ' + lube + ' -> ' + ('SAFE' if ok else 'UNSAFE: oil damages latex; choose water-based or silicone-based'))
print('Lubricant reduces condom breakage; it does not itself block HIV.')
print('See a clinician or an HIV testing service for advice on condoms and lubricants.')

Lubricant compatibility checker — edition: scientific
latex + water-based -> SAFE
latex + oil-based -> UNSAFE: oil damages latex; choose water-based or silicone-based
polyurethane + silicone-based -> SAFE
latex + silicone-based -> SAFE
Lubricant reduces condom breakage; it does not itself block HIV.

title: Testing Frequency Guidance
body:
Terminology and evidence frame. HIV is the virus (human immunodeficiency virus); AIDS is the syndrome (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) that can follow untreated HIV infection, so prevention in this database means interrupting HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the small number of stem-cell-transplant cases with sustained remission reported in the research literature are research exceptions involving high-risk procedures, not available cures. No prevention method described here is fully effective in real-world use; effectiveness figures below are conditional on adherence, correct use, and follow-up testing. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for individual advice.

Testing frequency guidance stratifies retesting intervals by risk. Baseline guidance in the United States recommends at least one HIV test for everyone aged 13 to 64 as part of routine care, with at least annual testing for sexually active gay and bisexual men and for other people at increased risk, and testing every three to six months for those at highest ongoing risk, such as people with multiple partners, partners of unknown status, or recent sexually transmitted infections. People who inject drugs and partners of people with HIV are included in routine retesting recommendations.

The rationale is epidemiological: incidence in a risk stratum determines the interval that keeps the undiagnosed period short. More frequent testing reduces the time from acquisition to diagnosis, which advances treatment initiation and TasP benefit and shortens the period of unknowing onward transmission. The interval is bounded below by the window period: testing more often than the window period adds little, and any test following a recent exposure requires a repeat after the window period regardless of schedule.

Effectiveness as prevention is mediated through diagnosis and linkage: testing itself does not reduce transmission, but it is the gateway to treatment and to partner services. Limits include testing fatigue, access gaps, and the failure mode in which frequent testers with negative results underuse other prevention. Risk-adapted schedules should be reviewed when risk changes, for example after a new partner, a condom failure, or a change in drug-use patterns.

Access includes clinical, community, and self-test routes, with self-testing useful for maintaining frequency between clinic visits provided confirmatory testing follows any reactive result. Anyone with a recent possible exposure should seek prompt assessment for PEP rather than waiting for the next scheduled test. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for a personal testing schedule.

for who, freq in PROFILES:

print('A test taken soon after an exposure may need repeating after the window period.')

title: Linkage to Care After a Positive Result
body:
Terminology and evidence frame. HIV is the virus (human immunodeficiency virus); AIDS is the syndrome (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) that can follow untreated HIV infection, so prevention in this database means interrupting HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the small number of stem-cell-transplant cases with sustained remission reported in the research literature are research exceptions involving high-risk procedures, not available cures. No prevention method described here is fully effective in real-world use; effectiveness figures below are conditional on adherence, correct use, and follow-up testing. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for individual advice.

Linkage to care is the process connecting a person with a confirmed HIV-positive result to antiretroviral therapy and longitudinal HIV care. The cascade steps are confirmatory testing under the laboratory algorithm, referral, first clinical visit, baseline laboratory assessment (including CD4 count, viral load, resistance testing where indicated, and screening for tuberculosis, hepatitis, and other sexually transmitted infections), ART initiation, and retention. WHO and CDC guidance support rapid ART initiation, including same-day start where the person is ready and no opportunistic infection requires deferral.

The mechanism is time-to-suppression: each week of delay prolongs viraemia, immune damage, and onward transmission risk, while rapid initiation shortens time to undetectable viral load and improves retention. Evidence from rapid-start trials and programs, including the RapIT and START trials' linkage findings, shows higher rates of viral suppression at twelve months with accelerated pathways than with multi-visit workups. Peer navigation, same-visit appointment booking, and active follow-up of missed appointments are the strongest linkage supports.

Effectiveness is bounded by system capacity and by stigma, transport, cost, and competing health needs, which produce the well-documented cascade drop-off between diagnosis and suppression. Linkage alone does not guarantee retention: adherence support, management of side effects and comorbidities, and mental-health and substance-use services determine long-term outcomes. A positive screening result without confirmatory testing is not a diagnosis, and linkage pathways must preserve that distinction.

Access is through HIV clinics, primary care, and community linkage programs, with costs covered by public programs in many settings. Limitations include workforce shortages, fragmented referral systems, and privacy concerns. Anyone with a positive result should be contacted promptly and offered a first appointment within days. See a clinician or an HIV testing service immediately after a positive result to arrange confirmation and care.

title: PrEP Adherence Support
body:
Terminology and evidence frame. HIV is the virus (human immunodeficiency virus); AIDS is the syndrome (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) that can follow untreated HIV infection, so prevention in this database means interrupting HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the small number of stem-cell-transplant cases with sustained remission reported in the research literature are research exceptions involving high-risk procedures, not available cures. No prevention method described here is fully effective in real-world use; effectiveness figures below are conditional on adherence, correct use, and follow-up testing. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for individual advice.

PrEP adherence support comprises the behavioral and systems interventions that maintain protective drug concentrations: habit formation, reminder systems, adherence counseling, side-effect management, and refill and appointment systems. For oral PrEP, protection correlates with drug levels: tenofovir diphosphate concentrations in dried blood spots consistent with four or more doses per week are associated with high protection for rectal exposure, while vaginal exposure requires closer to daily dosing. For injectable cabotegravir, adherence means keeping injections on schedule and managing the pharmacokinetic tail after discontinuation.

The mechanism is pharmacological: adherence maintains drug concentrations above the protective threshold at the exposure site. Interventions with the best evidence include counseling based on motivational interviewing, SMS reminders, pill organizers, and pharmacy-based refill synchronization. Objective adherence measures, such as dried blood spot tenofovir levels and injection records, outperform self-report for identifying people who need intensified support. Side effects, notably early nausea and headache with oral PrEP and injection-site reactions with cabotegravir, are the commonest adherence threats and are usually transient.

Effectiveness is indirect but decisive: adherence support does not itself prevent HIV, but it determines whether PrEP does. Limits include the inability of reminders to solve cost, supply, stigma, or clinic-access barriers, and the risk that adherence monitoring feels punitive unless framed as support. Discontinuation planning matters: after stopping injectable PrEP, alternative prevention is advised during the tail period of declining drug levels.

Access is through PrEP clinics, pharmacies, and telehealth programs, with peer support in many community programs. Anyone missing doses should contact their clinician promptly rather than stopping silently, since a plan can usually be made. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for adherence support, side-effect help, and follow-up testing.

title: Community Outreach Programs
body:
Terminology and evidence frame. HIV is the virus (human immunodeficiency virus); AIDS is the syndrome (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) that can follow untreated HIV infection, so prevention in this database means interrupting HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the small number of stem-cell-transplant cases with sustained remission reported in the research literature are research exceptions involving high-risk procedures, not available cures. No prevention method described here is fully effective in real-world use; effectiveness figures below are conditional on adherence, correct use, and follow-up testing. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for individual advice.

Community outreach programs deliver HIV prevention through peer-led, venue-based, and mobile modalities: community health workers and peer educators provide education, condom distribution, HIV testing (including rapid and self-test distribution), and active referral to PrEP, ART, and harm-reduction services in non-clinical settings. Target venues include social venues, shelters, workplaces, prisons' surrounding communities, and mobile units serving rural or underserved areas.

The mechanism is access and trust: outreach reduces geographic, temporal, financial, and stigma barriers that suppress clinic attendance, and peer delivery increases credibility and message acceptance. Evaluations associate outreach with higher testing uptake, higher first-time testing among previously unreached groups, and improved linkage when outreach is paired with same-day referral and navigation. Social-network strategies, in which peers recruit from their own networks, extend reach further into hidden populations.

Effectiveness is mediated entirely through linkage: outreach that does not connect people to testing, prevention, and care has little effect on incidence. Limits include funding instability, volunteer burnout, quality variation, and the difficulty of sustaining behavior change from brief contacts. Outreach must also manage confidentiality in small communities, where being seen at a testing event can itself carry stigma.

Access is through health departments, non-governmental organizations, and mobile programs, typically free at the point of use. Integration with clinics determines whether outreach converts contacts into sustained prevention. Anyone unable to reach a clinic should ask a testing service about outreach options. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for links to community programs.
